hook: You know Matthew 11:28. But did you know it comes right after Jesus denounced the towns where he had done most of his miracles?
story:
Jesus has just had a hard run of words, and a hard run of answers.

John the Baptizer is “in the prison”. He has heard about the works of Christ, and he sends two of his disciples with a question: “Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?” Jesus does not argue. He tells them to go and report what they hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the poor have good news preached to them.

Then he turns to the crowd and says how people have treated both men. John came neither eating nor drinking, and they said he had a demon. Jesus came eating and drinking, and they called him a “friend of tax collectors and sinners”. Whatever he did, someone found fault.

Next he does something startling. He begins to denounce “the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they didn’t repent.” Chorazin, Bethsaida, Capernaum: the places where people had seen the most were the places he names.

Then he prays. He thanks his Father that these things are hidden “from the wise and understanding” and revealed “to infants.” And in the very next words, the verse: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.”

The text does not tell us how Jesus felt in any of this, and we should not guess. It records what he did: after a chapter of questions, rejections and warnings, he invites the tired to come to him.

moment:
Jesus is speaking to the crowds, as he has been since he began to talk about John. The people he addresses are those who “labor” and are “heavily burdened”. A related word turns up later in Matthew, when Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees “bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them.” Long hears the invitation against that background, as a contrast with the Pharisees.

Then comes the second half of the call: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” A yoke links animals at their work, and Long notes that in the writing of Jesus’ day it was a picture for a burden, for obedience and for subordination. The one who invites does not say the load is nothing. He says, “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
around:
Just before the verse, Jesus says that “No one knows the Son, except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father, except the Son and he to whom the Son desires to reveal him.” The invitation comes straight out of that claim: he is the one who reveals the Father, so he is the one to come to.

Just after it, the chapter turns to the Sabbath. His disciples pluck heads of grain on the Sabbath day and the Pharisees object. The question of whose burdens are being carried, and how, is immediately tested.
after:
In the very next chapter Matthew shows what taking Jesus’ side costs. When the Pharisees object to the disciples picking grain on the Sabbath, Jesus answers that “one greater than the temple is here” and that “the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.” Then, after he heals a man with a withered hand, “the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how they might destroy him.” Jesus withdraws, and “Great multitudes followed him; and he healed them all,”

Later in Acts, when the early church argued over whether non-Jewish believers had to keep the law, Peter asked why anyone would put “a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear” on them. He added that “we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus”

The verse also found its way into worship. The North American Anglican page explains that in the 1662 Book of Common Prayer it is the first of the Comfortable Words, said right after confession and absolution, in the old English that says travail and refresh.

About 1845, in Kelso, Scotland, the minister Horatius Bonar wrote a hymn that opens with the voice of Jesus saying this verse. Its first pencil draft was nearly the hymn as we sing it now, but it was not printed until 1850, in a book of three stanzas without music, and in 1857 under the title The Voice from Galilee. The Hymnology Archive says Bonar meant such hymns for his church’s Sunday school, because his Free Church of Scotland sang only psalm paraphrases in worship.
readings:
One reading, as Phillip J. Long gives it, hears Jesus setting his yoke against the heavy extra rules the Pharisees laid on people. On this reading the yoke is Jesus’ own teaching, and taking it up means becoming his disciple.

A second reading hears an echo of Jeremiah. There the LORD tells a people to ask for the old paths and walk in them, and promises that they “will find rest for your souls.” The same words stand in Matthew’s verse 29. In Jeremiah the people answer that they will not walk in it, and some scholars, Long cites Nolland, see Jesus calling people back to that good way.

A third reading finds a parallel in the book of Sirach, which also invites people to put their neck under the yoke of wisdom. Long notes the difference: Sirach calls the uneducated to learn, while Jesus calls the weary to rest.

A fourth is the way the Prayer Book later used the verse, as a word of comfort to hear before communion. These readings do not have to compete, and the sources here do not name a winner.
argued:
In the English Prayer Book, this verse became the first of four sentences read to the congregation before communion, called the Comfortable Words. The page that describes them quotes the clergyman Thomas Comber, who wrote in the 1600s about why those four were chosen: [[comber]]

A modern commentator is careful about the other half of the verse. Phillip J. Long, reading the same passage, does not let the word rest cover over the word yoke: [[long]] Both writers take the invitation seriously. They differ on how much weight to put on comfort and how much on following.
point: Matthew 11:28 is not a free-floating line about tiredness. It is spoken to people already carrying loads, after Jesus has been questioned, refused and criticized, and it asks them to come to a person and learn from him. The rest it names is joined to that yoke.
lesson:
Notice who the invitation is for. It is not for the strong, the organized or the ones who have it together. It is for the tired, the people carrying more than they can manage. If that is you today, you do not have to clean yourself up before you read this verse.

Notice too that it is spoken to a person, not to a program. Jesus does not hand out a better plan. He says, “Come to me”. For a reader who believes, that can mean praying today in plain words, naming the weight, and then opening Matthew 11 and reading the whole chapter, not only its best-known line.

The yoke matters as well. Jesus describes himself as gentle and humble in heart, and he still speaks of a yoke. Following him is not a life without weight. For a reader who does not share the faith, the verse can still be read for what it is: an old and honest answer to being worn out by demands, and an open door you are free to walk through or not.

echoes.note: In a psalm full of betrayal, the answer is “Cast your burden on the LORD”. Like Matthew 11:28, it asks the weary to hand the load over instead of carrying it alone.
God calls “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters!” to people who spend their labor on what does not satisfy. It is the same open invitation to the tired and empty.
John writes that loving God means keeping his commandments, and adds “His commandments are not grievous.” That matches Jesus saying that his burden is light.
